source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Fine-Tuned Vision Transformers on Distorted Images: Decoding Attention Head Behavior for Transparent and Trustworthy AI

record.file_problem: The provided text appears complete. It contains some page-break and formatting artifacts, but they do not prevent reading the relevant sections.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines attention heads, not individual neurons. Its attention-map findings therefore do not test the neuron claims or versions listed.
record.gate_note: The paper reports observations about attention-head maps, including heads it calls monosemantic or polysemantic. These are not measurements of neuron responses, so the findings are recorded under fits_no_version rather than linked to a claim version. The attention-head ablation results concern task performance, not polysemanticity, and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study inspects attention maps of ViT attention heads and labels heads monosemantic or polysemantic by where they attend. It never measures neuron responses to unrelated inputs, so it tests no version of the neuron claim. The introduction restates the superposition explanation (V3) citing Olah et al. 2020, but does not test it. The ablation results measure task importance, not polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right, with three refinements. The authors conclude that intermediate-layer heads (6-11) are monosemantic chirp localizers. Some early heads (1-4) are monosemantic but detect non-task features. Diffuse heads such as L12H12 are called polysemantic. Ablation shows early-layer heads matter little (mean 0.11% MSE increase) and deeper heads matter more (e.g. layer 6, mean 0.34%). The authors frame all this as functional specialization in ViTs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses normalized attention-map visualization and ablation of attention-head weights in a fine-tuned ViT, rather than measuring individual neuron responses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported attention-map patterns differ by layer and head.

fits_no_version.finding: In a LoRA-fine-tuned ViT on synthetic spectrograms, some heads in layers 4 and 6-11 attend only to the chirp. Layer 12 Head 12 attends diffusely to multiple irrelevant regions. Several heads in layers 1-4 attend to specific non-task features such as text, color bars, edges and corners.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention heads in vision transformers vary between spatially focused, single-feature attention patterns and diffuse, multi-region patterns.

record.problems: The attention-map interpretations are qualitative and are not reported as neuron measurements. The paper gives no quantitative criterion for classifying heads as monosemantic or polysemantic, and the listed attention-map claims have no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports ablation-related MSE changes and prediction distributions in the Results section and Figures 3–4, but these measure head importance for task performance rather than polysemanticity or the claim versions, so they were not included.

untested.parts: No individual neurons in image classifiers are examined; only ViT attention-head maps.
No language models or MLP neurons are studied.
Superposition is asserted in the introduction (citing Olah et al.) but not tested.
Not addressed; the paper gives no quantitative scoring of head 'semanticity'.

record.verdict_notes: Single-author preprint. The mono/polysemantic terms are applied to attention heads by visual inspection only, so none of the neuron-level versions apply. The reader's T6/discusses classification and the 'none' links on all rows are correct. The ablation results are rightly left out as task importance, not polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies ViT attention heads, not whether individual neurons in image classifiers respond to several unrelated inputs.
No transformer language models or MLP neurons are examined.
The paper does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
The paper does not test initialization, regularization, training noise, or whether there is enough capacity for every feature.
It does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons across architectures, activation functions, or regularization settings, nor the associated performance tradeoff.
Attention-map patterns are not tests of whether polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
The paper does not compare activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

rows.operation_detail: Inspected attention maps and identified heads described as attending exclusively to chirp regions.

conditions.value: synthetic spectrograms containing chirps and non-relevant regions

rows.value: Only specific heads in layers 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 were reported to attend solely to the chirp region.
rows.note: This is a finding about attention heads, not neurons.
rows.check: Attention-head localization, not a neuron measurement. No count of heads per layer and no criterion are reported.

rows.subject: fine-tuned ViT model
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the attention map of Layer 6, Head 4.
rows.value: The attention map was described as focused precisely on the chirp region and as monosemantic.
rows.note: This is an attention-head finding, not a neuron measurement.

rows.subject: fine-tuned ViT model
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the attention map of Layer 12, Head 12.
rows.value: The head was described as polysemantic, with attention distributed across multiple irrelevant regions rather than focused exclusively on the chirp.
rows.note: The paper's label applies to an attention head and its attention map, not to an individual neuron.
rows.check: 'Polysemantic' here means one head's attention spreads across several spatial regions. That is not a neuron responding to unrelated inputs. The label comes from qualitative inspection of one example map, with no criterion stated.
